plan.contextChunk: This figure shows the unit circle with a fixed angle c and a variable angle x measured from the positive horizontal axis, illustrating the continuity of the sine and cosine functions. Point Q(cos c, sin c) is marked in blue at angle c, and point P(cos x, sin x) is marked in red at angle x; an arrow indicates that P moves toward Q as x approaches c. A caption box at the bottom reads: As x approaches c the point P approaches the point Q. The figure provides a geometric motivation for the limits lim_{x->c} sin x = sin c and lim_{x->c} cos x = cos c, establishing that sin and cos are continuous at every point c.

interactions.label: Angle x (point P)
interactions.teaches: Dragging x slides P along the circle and shrinks or grows the shaded sector; as x gets close to c the red radius, the sector, and the gap between P and Q all collapse toward zero, making the limit lim_{x->c} (cos x, sin x) = (cos c, sin c) visually obvious

interactions.label: x -> c from both sides
interactions.teaches: The self-playing sweep drives x toward c first from below and then from above, so the learner sees P converge to Q from both directions — the two-sided limit behavior that underlies continuity

demo_steps.title: Two angles, one circle
demo_steps.narration: A fixed angle c places Q(cos c, sin c) in blue and a variable angle x places P(cos x, sin x) in red; the purple sector between their radii measures the angular gap between them.

demo_steps.title: Slide x toward c
demo_steps.narration: Drag the x slider up toward c: P travels along the circle toward Q, the red radius rotates onto the dark radius, and the shaded sector shrinks to nothing — the coordinates (cos x, sin x) are converging to (cos c, sin c).

demo_steps.title: Move the target c
demo_steps.narration: Now drag the c slider to a new angle: Q, both radii, the sector, the angle arcs, and the labels all relocate together, confirming the limit-and-continuity argument works at any c, not just the one pictured.

demo_steps.title: Approach from both sides
demo_steps.narration: Play the animation: x sweeps into c from below and then from above, so P closes on Q from both directions around the circle — exactly the two-sided limit lim_{x->c} that makes sine and cosine continuous everywhere.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Continuity of sine and cosine is just the fact that the point (cos x, sin x) slides continuously around the unit circle as the angle x varies, so x -> c forces the coordinates to approach (cos c, sin c) from both sides.

authoredInteractions:
- Slider for angle x: animate point P along the unit circle toward fixed point Q(cos c, sin c) and watch the shaded sector shrink, illustrating the squeeze theorem setup

authoredContext:
Recall from trigonometry that the graphs of sin x and cos x are drawn as continuous curves. We will not formally prove that these functions are continuous, but we can motivate this fact by letting c be a fixed angle in radian measure and x a variable angle in radian measure. If, as illustrated in Figure 1.6.1, the angle x approaches the angle c, then the point P(cos x,sin x) moves along the unit circle toward Q(cos c,sin c), and the coordinates of P approach the
corresponding coordinates of Q. This implies that
lim
x→c
sin x = sin c and limx→c
cos x = cos c (1)
Thus, sin x and cos x are continuous at the arbitrary point c; that is, these functions are continuous everywhere.
